facts.statement: Preondactylus lived approximately 217 to 214 million years ago in what is now Italy.
facts.quote: Preondactylus is a genus of long-tailed pterosaurs from the Late Triassic (Carnian-Norian or late Norian, about 217–214 million years ago) that inhabited what is now Italy.

facts.statement: The species Preondactylus buffarinii was discovered by Nando Buffarini in 1982 in the Preone valley of the Italian Alps.
facts.quote: It contains a single known species, Preondactylus buffarinii, which was discovered by Nando Buffarini in 1982 at the Forni Dolostone near Udine in the Preone valley of the Italian Alps.

facts.statement: The original fossil slab containing the first specimen was accidentally broken into pieces during extraction.
facts.quote: When Buffarini first discovered Preondactylus, the thin slab of bituminous, dolomitic limestone containing the fossil was accidentally broken into pieces while being extracted.

facts.statement: Researchers studied the first specimen using a silicone rubber cast made from a negative imprint on stone, as the original bone was lost.
facts.quote: All that was left was a negative imprint on the stone, of which a silicone rubber cast was made to allow for subsequent study of the otherwise lost remains.

facts.statement: A second specimen, MFSN-1891, was found in 1984 approximately 150 to 200 meters deeper in the strata than the original discovery.
facts.quote: A second, disarticulated specimen, MFSN-1891, was found at the same locale in 1984 about 150 – 200 m deeper into the strata than the original find.

facts.statement: Evidence suggests the second specimen was preserved inside the gastric pellet of a predatory fish that vomited it up after eating the pterosaur.
facts.quote: The second specimen appears to have been preserved in the gastric pellet of a predatory fish, which had consumed the pterosaur and vomited up the indigestible pieces that would later fossilize.

facts.statement: A third specimen, MFSN 25161, consists of a partial skull that lacks the lower jaws.
facts.quote: A third specimen is MFSN 25161, a partial skull, lacking the lower jaws.

facts.statement: Preondactylus possessed single-cusp teeth with one point on each tooth.
facts.quote: Preondactylus had single cusp teeth, meaning they had one point on each tooth.

facts.statement: The widely spaced, pointed teeth of Preondactylus did not occlude, resulting in an absence of tooth wear.
facts.quote: Because its teeth were monocuspid, pointed, and widely spaced apart, they did not occlude; tooth wear was thus absent in Preondactylus.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Preondactylus ate fish, insects, or both, as its tooth structure could indicate either or both diets.
facts.quote: Its diet either consisted of fish, insects or both, but there is still debate going on as the tooth structure could indicate either diet (or both).

facts.statement: Although Preondactylus had short wings considered a primitive feature, it was a fully developed flier.
facts.quote: The short wings are considered a "primitive" feature for pterosaurs, but Preondactylus was a fully developed flier.

facts.statement: Preondactylus was described and named by Rupert Wild in 1984.
facts.quote: The species was described and named by Rupert Wild in 1984.

facts.statement: Rupert Wild initially classified Preondactylus within Rhamphorhynchidae, but it was later understood to be much more basal.
facts.quote: Rupert classified the new species within Rhamphorhynchidae, of which group very old species are known such as Dorygnathus, but soon it was understood the form was much more basal.

facts.statement: David Unwin identified Preondactylus as the most basal pterosaur and used it to define the node for the clade Pterosauria.
facts.quote: A cladistic analysis by David Unwin found Preondactylus as the most basal pterosaur, and the species was accordingly used by him for a node clade definition of the clade Pterosauria.

facts.statement: Some phylogenetic analyses have placed Preondactylus in a somewhat more derived position than the most basal.
facts.quote: Other analyses however, have found a somewhat more derived position for Preondactylus.

facts.statement: Preondactylus was approximately the size of a pigeon.
facts.quote: Preondactylus tenía el tamaño aproximado de una paloma.

facts.statement: Preondactylus had short wings with a total wingspan of only 45 centimeters and relatively long legs.
facts.quote: Tenía alas cortas, cuya envergadura total era de solo 45 centímetros, y patas relativamente largas.

facts.statement: A cladistic analysis by David Unwin found Preondactylus to be the most basal pterosaur, leading him to use it to define the Pterosauria clade node.
facts.quote: Un análisis cladístico hecho por David Unwin encontró que Preondactylus como el pterosaurio más basal, y la especie fue de acuerdo con esto usada por él para definir el nodo del clado Pterosauria.

facts.statement: Other analyses have considered a somewhat more advanced position for Preondactylus within the suborder Pterodactylia.
facts.quote: Otros análisis sin embargo, han considerado una posición algo más avanzada para Preondactylus,el infraorden Pterodactylia.

rejected.quote: The holotype had a wingspan of 45 cm, while a larger referred specimen is estimated to have a wingspan of 1.5 m.

rejected.statement: It is debated whether the second specimen MFSN-1891 belongs to Preondactylus, as increased knowledge of Triassic pterosaur variability suggests it may not be a pterosaur at all.
rejected.quote: More detailed knowledge of the variability of Triassic pterosaurs has made the identification of this specimen as Preondactylus uncertain, and it may even be that the remains are not those of a pterosaur at all.
